evidence.package_quote: Determining the oxidation state of copper in materials is critical for catalysts, energy devices, and nanomaterials.
The approach uses a dataset of simulated Cu L₂,₃-edge XAS spectra curated from the Materials Project and augmented with synthetic mixed‑valence spectra generated by linear combination.
A random forest regressor with 500 trees is trained on the training features and oxidation state labels.

The model is then applied to the test set to produce per‑sample predictions (mean oxidation state and standard deviation across trees), and overall regression metrics (R² and RMSE) are computed from those predictions.

Core-level spectroscopy (EELS and XAS) encodes oxidation state information, but traditional analysis relies on expert spectral matching to known standards, which is time-consuming, sensitive to experimental variations, and not scalable.
